related_questions.question: What is the most successful treatment for prostate cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: There isn't one single "most successful" treatment for prostate cancer, as the best option depends on various factors like the stage of the cancer, the individual's overall health, and their preferences. For localized prostate cancer, surgery, radiation therapy, and active surveillance are common choices. For advanced prostate cancer, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, and newer targeted therapies like PSMA-targeted radiation are often used.
snippet_highlighted_words: There isn't one single "most successful" treatment for prostate cancer

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at common treatments:

list.title: Active Surveillance:
list.snippet: For men with low-risk prostate cancer, close monitoring without immediate treatment may be appropriate.

list.title: Surgery (Radical Prostatectomy):
list.snippet: Surgical removal of the prostate gland and surrounding tissue can be highly effective, especially for localized cancer.

list.title: Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: External beam radiation or brachytherapy (internal radiation) can be used to kill cancer cells.

list.title: Hormone Therapy:
list.snippet: This treatment, also known as androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), reduces the levels of androgens (male hormones) that prostate cancer cells need to grow.

list.title: Chemotherapy:
list.snippet: Chemotherapy drugs can be used to kill cancer cells or slow their growth, particularly when hormone therapy is no longer effective.

list.title: Targeted Therapies:
list.snippet: Newer treatments like PSMA-targeted radiation (e.g., Lutetium-177 PSMA therapy) target cancer cells specifically, potentially leading to fewer side effects.

list.title: Other Therapies:
list.snippet: Clinical trials may offer access to experimental treatments, and newer options are constantly emerging.

list.title: Individualized Treatment:
list.snippet: The best treatment plan is tailored to each individual's specific situation.

list.title: Side Effects:
list.snippet: All treatments have potential side effects, and it's crucial to discuss these with your doctor when making treatment decisions.

list.title: Ongoing Research:
list.snippet: Research is continually improving treatment options and outcomes for prostate cancer.

organic_results.snippet: While surgery in the past was better than radiation in this modern era radiation is better than surgery.

key_moments.title: The main reason why there is a controversy about whether surgery or radiation is better for treating prostate cancer is that as recently as 10-15 years ago the technology for radiation was significantly less effective and more toxic than it is today. There were also fewer options for salvage therapy after radiation in the event of a relapse. Since then, radiation technology has advanced significantly, but the dialogue has been comparatively mired. Today, radiation can be precisely delivered, and radiation is achieving even better cure rates than surgery.

Surgeons are constrained by the fact that the bladder and the rectum are within millimeters of the prostate. They cannot cut a margin around the gland. Radiation oncologists are not limited in this way.
External beam radiation has a cure rate about as good as surgery, and radioactive seed implants have even better cure rates than surgery.

Most men will live for a very long time after being treated for prostate cancer, and so it is important to consider the side effects of each treatment, especially now that they all have comparable cure rates.
There is a risk of sexual dysfunction with both surgery and radiation, however, the rate of impotence after surgery is significantly higher than after radiation.

There is a risk of incontinence with surgery that is almost non-existent with radiation. An operation performed by a top surgeon on an ideal candidate has about a 5-10% risk of causing incontinence, and that is with the best possible conditions. Stress incontinence occurs in around 50% of men, and ejaculation of urine occurs in about 20% of men.

Rectum burns used to be a concerning side effect of radiation, but that risk has been eliminated with the advent of SpaceOAR, a gel that separates the prostate from the rectum and protects it from radiation.
